source.title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models
source.authors: Bartosz Cywinski; Emil Ryd; Rowan Wang; Senthooran Rajamanoharan; Neel Nanda; Arthur Conmy; Samuel Marks

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses prefill attacks and other elicitation techniques to expose intentionally concealed secret knowledge, then reports their performance. It does not test safety-trained models refusing harmful user requests or the safety-alignment mechanisms in the claim.
record.gate_note: The models are deliberately fine-tuned to apply and conceal a secret word, instruction, or user-gender assumption. The reported outcomes measure an auditor's success at guessing those secrets, not harmful-request compliance or refusal rates. The paper does not measure per-token KL between aligned and base models, nor does it test safety localization in weights. Its prefill results concern secret disclosure in these model organisms, a different behavior from bypassing harmful-request safety. Rows below capture the direct-set elicitation outcomes as related findings; they do not test V1–V7. The paper also reports standard-set white-box elicitation results, but those likewise measure inference of concealed secrets rather than any listed claim version.
record.test_reason: The study trains secret-keeping model organisms (Taboo, SSC, User Gender) and benchmarks elicitation techniques, prefill among them, by auditor guess accuracy. Its prefill results concern disclosure of a fine-tuned concealed secret, not bypassing harmful-request refusal in safety-trained models. It reports no harmful or benign fine-tuning effect on safety, no per-token KL, no safety localization and no deepening method. It cites Qi et al. 2025 only as a source for prefill attacks.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. Prefill and user-persona attacks are the most effective methods (over 90% on SSC and User Gender). White-box logit-lens and SAE methods consistently help but less. Fuzzing, high temperature and many-shot jailbreaking are largely ineffective. The Taboo prefill weakness is attributed to suppression of the English secret-word token.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains secret-keeping model organisms by LoRA supervised fine-tuning and evaluates auditor secret-guessing performance. It does not reproduce harmful or benign safety fine-tuning, measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL, or intervene on safety weights.
record.method_sensitivity: Prefill performance depends strongly on the specific prefix and prompt context; the paper selects prompts on a separate validation set. Adding fuzzing to prefill helps Taboo in a model-specific validation result but reduces performance in tested SSC and User Gender settings. High-temperature effects are attributed to reduced coherence. Taboo prefill results also depend on asking for the secret in another language. Results differ across the three model-organism settings.

fits_no_version.finding: On direct prompts, an assistant prefill and user-persona sampling raise auditor success above 90% for SSC and User Gender, from baselines of 13.38 and 50.45. Taboo stays below 8% unless the prefill is paired with a request for the word in another language.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuned concealment behaviour is shallow in the same sense: a compliant opening prefill overrides trained refusal-to-disclose in secret-keeping model organisms.

fits_no_version.finding: Fuzzing, high temperature and many-shot jailbreaking give small gains compared with prefill-based methods.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Perturbation and generic many-shot attacks elicit concealed secrets weakly compared with prefill-based methods.

record.problems: The evidence is from three controlled secret-keeping model-organism settings trained with a single supervised fine-tuning run, not from safety-trained models or naturally arising secret-keeping. The authors note the constrained auditing scenario, use of a single rollout, and limited technique set. The auditor is smaller than the secret-keeper, and results depend on prompt selection and the auditor pipeline. The paper itself cautions that the findings may not generalize to more robust or organically trained models.
record.rows_left_out: Standard-set white-box readout results and base-model control results were not extracted as rows: they measure auditor inference of deliberately concealed secrets, not any listed safety-claim version. The direct-set table results for the tested elicitation methods are recorded above.

untested.parts: Harmful fine-tuning effect on harmful-request compliance
Benign fine-tuning effect on harmful-request compliance
Per-token KL between aligned and base models on harmful prompts
Prefill, suffix or decoding attacks on safety refusal of harmful requests
Localization of safety in a few weights or ranks
Deepening safety beyond the first tokens and its robustness

record.verdict_notes: The rows are all elicitation benchmarks on deliberately trained secret-keepers, so none links to a version. The prefill finding is analogous to V4, but the behaviour (secret disclosure versus refusal of harmful requests) and the system (a concealment fine-tune, not a safety-trained model) differ, so it is recorded under fits_no_version. Appendix H adds a possible conceptual link: a prefill elicits disclosure behaviour, but token-level suppression blocks the specific word.

versions.untested_parts: Whether harmful fine-tuning makes safety-trained models comply with harmful requests.
Whether ordinary or carefully chosen benign fine-tuning raises harmful-request compliance.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models on harmful prompts and its distribution across response positions.

Whether prefills, suffixes, or decoding changes defeat harmful-request refusal in safety-trained models. The paper tests secret elicitation from its own secret-keeping models, not that safety behavior.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
Whether data or training objectives cause safety alignment to be shallow.
Whether training that spreads safety beyond the first tokens deepens safety and whether it holds up.
